articles.body: 📅 November 13, 2026 • Source: Hugging Face ggml-org has shipped llama.cpp v1.0.0 together with ggml v1.0.0 , both published on November 13, 2026, per the ggml-org team. The stack that powers local LLM inference on everything from laptops to enterprise servers has relied on rolling 0.x numbering for the 3.5 years since the project began, per the team's Hugging Face post. The 1.0.0 tag marks the moment the public API becomes a managed contract rather than a moving target. Per the release notes, llama.cpp v1.0.0 is the LLM inference engine written in C and C++ (libllama), while ggml v1.0.0 is the machine learning tensor library underneath it (libggml).

articles.body: A webhook handler can pass every signature check and still reject the event because it looks too old. The fix people reach for first is setting the tolerance to 0, which makes the error disappear. Stripe's docs name that as a mistake. This post covers what the timestamp in the Stripe-Signature header is for, what Stripe says about the default tolerance, what it recommends for server clocks, and why retries aren't the cause. Every claim links to the doc it comes from (see Sources at the end).

articles.body: Jules de Google ya no acepta trabajo nuevo. El agente de código asíncrono de Google Labs quedó en modo de solo lectura el 11 de noviembre y cerrará por completo el 31 de diciembre de 2026. Quedan 48 días para exportar ajustes, memorias y sesiones antes de que el servicio se apague, y esa exportación es la única copia de lo que Jules guardaba fuera de GitHub. El aviso llegó el 29 de octubre en el registro de cambios oficial del producto, en la entrada «Jules Turndown». Google explicó ahí que el cierre forma parte de su trabajo para unificar sus esfuerzos de programación con agentes. Las sesiones pudieron terminarse hasta el 11 de noviembre; desde ese día la herramienta solo permite mirar, y así seguirá hasta fin de año.

articles.title: I saw Saturn’s rings in seconds with the Celestron StarSense Explorer 150mm Tabletop Dobsonian telescope — full review
articles.excerpt: Celestron’s StarSense Explorer tech makes this 150mm Dobsonian so easy to operate — but its tabletop design makes me wonder whether beginners should go bigger.
articles.body: Saturn was only a night past its annual opposition when I pointed the Celestron StarSense Explorer 150mm Tabletop Dobsonian straight at it. The planet was at its biggest and brightest of the year, the seeing was good and its famous rings were visibly opening up after appearing edge-on from Earth in recent years. It was an obvious target for a new telescope. Finding it took seconds. After selecting Saturn in Celestron’s StarSense Explorer app, I followed the on-screen arrows as I moved the telescope across the sky. As I got closer, the app zoomed in until a bullseye turned green. I looked through the supplied 25mm eyepiece, then swapped to the 10mm to see a pale yellow Saturn at 75x magnification, with its rings sharply defined and its giant moon Titan visible in orbit.

You can watch it live here at Space.com, courtesy of ULA, or directly via the company . Coverage will start 20 minutes before liftoff. (Image credit: ULA) Vulcan Centaur is the successor to ULA's workhorse Atlas V rocket, which has just a half-dozen launches left on its manifest. Vulcan debuted in January 2024 and has flown three more times since.

articles.title: Silicon Valley claims to know the future. So why did it get the midterms so wrong?
articles.excerpt: The self-styled visionaries of Silicon Valley, leaders like OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman and SpaceX boss Elon Musk, have built careers claiming to see the future. Long-term vision is currency: Me…
articles.body: The self-styled visionaries of Silicon Valley, leaders like OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman and SpaceX boss Elon Musk, have built careers claiming to see the future. Long-term vision is currency: Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg built a 10-year road map for Facebook in 2016, and Google famously told investors before its public offering that it was unconcerned with short-term results. And yet there they all were, a mere five weeks before the midterm elections, gathered at the White House to smile for photos with President Trump and sign on to his “Super Intelligence” agenda. Even by the diminished standards of today’s corporate governance, this was a shockingly foolish decision.

articles.title: 'Don't panic': SpaceX pens familiar message on Starship ahead of historic double-catch test flight
articles.excerpt: SpaceX has inked a familiar phrase on the Starship rocket that will fly a historic mission today (Nov. 13) — "Don't panic." And the company has invoked those words before.
articles.body: SpaceX has a message for itself, and for the spacecraft set to make history today (Nov. 13): Don't panic. The company's Starship megarocket will conduct its 15th test flight this afternoon, a landmark liftoff that will feature the first-ever attempt to catch both of its stages with its launch tower's "chopstick" arms. On Thursday (Nov. 12), SpaceX rolled the Flight 15 upper stage, a vehicle known as Ship 42, out to the launch pad at its Starbase site in South Texas to prep. The company shared photos of the move on X , and in two of those shots we can see some intriguing words inked on the spacecraft: "Don't panic." Another look at Ship 42 at the pad on Nov. 12.
